vignette:
He remembers the light first. Grey morning light slanting through the kitchen window, the smell of tea brewing, and then the sound of his mother’s voice, sharp and thin. He is seven years old, standing in the doorway of the small house near the sugarcane fields. His father is home from the fields early, still carrying the machete. The noise comes next—a chair scraping, a plate breaking, his mother backing against the wall. He stands frozen, watching his father’s hand rise and fall. He does not scream. He does not run. He just stands there, eyes wide, as the grey light turns into something heavy and permanent. His mother’s eyes meet his for a moment, and she whispers, “Go outside, Kwame.” He goes. He stands in the yard, trembling, listening to the sounds he cannot unhear.

Now he is forty-five. He still lives near the fields, but in a different country, a different province. He works for a large fruit farm, tending rows of apple trees from dawn until the heat breaks. The work is steady, solitary. He likes the quiet, the repetition of pruning and picking, the way the trees do not ask anything of him. But the quiet is never really quiet. In the early mornings, when the mist hangs low between the rows, his chest tightens without reason. He catches himself holding his breath, listening. For what? He cannot say. The clang of a metal bucket might send a jolt through his spine, and he stops, hand over his heart, until the rhythm settles.

He does not talk about his childhood. When his partner, a woman he has been with for six years, asks about his family, he shakes his head and says, “Long time ago. Nothing good to remember.” She has learned not to press. At night, he sleeps on his side of the bed, rigid, waiting. The nightmares come two or three times a week: the same kitchen, the same grey light, the same sound of something breaking. He wakes with his fists clenched, drenched in sweat, unable to fall back asleep. He gets up before dawn, makes tea, and stares at the wall until it is time to go to the fields.

During the day, he works hard—harder than the younger men. He checks the branches for signs of disease, pulls weeds by hand, never allows himself a pause. If he stops, the images return: his mother’s face, his father’s hands. He has learned to fill the silence with labor. His supervisor once joked that he is the most productive man on the crew. Kwame forced a smile, but inside he felt nothing. Praise feels hollow, like a stone dropped into a deep well. He does not feel proud. He feels tired.

His relationship suffers in small, quiet ways. His partner wants to hold his hand, to talk about the future. He pulls away. Not because he does not care—he does, deeply—but because closeness feels dangerous. Intimacy means vulnerability, and vulnerability means the past can get in. When she touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinches. He apologizes, but the apology is thin. He cannot explain why a sudden touch makes him want to run. He cannot explain that he is always on alert, listening for a sound that never comes.

The world feels thin to him, like a skin stretched over a wound. The apple trees are beautiful in spring, but he does not see their pink blossoms—he sees branches that could become weapons. He hears a loud truck backfire in the distance and his heart slams. He avoids group meals, crowded places, any setting where he cannot watch the door. He sits alone under a tree at lunch, eating his bread in silence, scanning the horizon.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his partner, not the doctor he saw once for his high blood pressure. The memories live in his body—in the knots of his shoulders, in the way he startles at a raised voice, in the sleepless hours before dawn. He goes to work. He comes home. He sits in the dark. Some days, he wonders if this is just how life is. Some days, he wonders if he will ever feel safe.
